research_publication.en: Any AI use in researching or writing a doctoral thesis requires prior approval from the supervisor(s) and supervisory committee, and approval for research does not cover writing. claim-university-of-toronto-001.text: For the doctoral thesis specifically, the University of Toronto School of Graduate Studies requires that the use of generative AI tools in any aspect of researching or writing the thesis be done with the prior approval of the supervisor(s) and supervisory committee. Students remain responsible for any AI-generated content in the thesis and must be able to describe and defend any AI use at the final oral examination.

evidence.quote: Students are responsible for any content generated by AI that they include in their thesis.
evidence.location: Doctoral thesis; lines 69-69 of captured page text

evidence.quote: Students must be able to describe and defend any use of generative AI, as well as the contents of the thesis during their final oral examination.

claim-university-of-toronto-002.text: Where approved generative AI use contributes to a University of Toronto doctoral thesis, the thesis must appropriately cite and describe that use so the reader can tell which tools were used, and how and why. Approval to use AI in research does not extend to writing: graduate students must separately seek and document supervisor and committee approval for AI use in writing. SGS does not regulate master's theses, Major Research Papers or comprehensive exams; graduate units set those rules, while the Code of Behaviour and research-misconduct framework still apply.

evidence.quote: Careful attention must be paid in the thesis to appropriately citing and describing any use of generative AI tools in the research process. It must be clear to the reader which generative AI tools were used, as well as how and why they were used.
evidence.location: Doctoral thesis; lines 67-67 of captured page text

evidence.quote: Graduate students must seek and document approval from their supervisors and committees for the use of generative AI in writing even if they already have approval to use generative AI tools in their research.

draft-claim-uoft-code-fabricated-referen.text: The 2025 Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters also makes it an offence knowingly to submit academic work containing a purported statement of fact or reference to a source that has been concocted (an offence depending on knowledge, including where the student ought reasonably to have known; not every AI error is automatically an offence). When an instructor has reasonable grounds to believe an offence was committed, they must inform the student immediately, give reasons and invite a discussion, normally held synchronously; nothing the student says in that discussion may be used in evidence at a hearing. The dean or chair must tell the student they may seek advice or be represented and are not obliged to make any statement. Sanctions available at divisional level include up to 12 months' suspension (up to 24 with Provost approval); suspension of up to five years or a recommendation of expulsion are for the University Tribunal.

draft-claim-uoft-learning-aid-use.text: The University of Toronto FAQ (updated October 2026) says undergraduate and graduate students may use generative AI tools as learning aids, for example to summarize information or test their understanding, in a manner similar to consulting books, peers or a tutor. Such uses are generally acceptable even if an instructor has said AI is not otherwise permitted in the course, and typically do not need to be cited or disclosed. If students use AI-generated information that would normally require citation (quoting, paraphrasing or reproducing text or ideas), they must cite it according to U of T Libraries guidance or the instructor's directions. Learning-aid use is distinct from using AI to complete marked work.

evidence.quote: Undergraduate and graduate students may use GenAI tools as learning aids, for example, to summarize information or test their understanding of a topic. These tools should be used in a manner similar to consulting library books, online sources, peers, or a tutor. Such uses are generally acceptable even if an instructor has stated that AI tools are not otherwise permitted in the course. These uses typically do not need to be cited or disclosed.

A Privacy Impact Assessment is required wherever an unvetted tool collects personally identifying information, typically taking four to eight weeks.

evidence.quote: Students must be able to opt out. You cannot require students to accept a third party’s terms or hand over personal data or intellectual property. If the tool is part of a required activity or assessment, you must provide a viable alternative for students who decline.
evidence.location: Using non-supported tools; lines 195-195 of captured page text

This process typically takes four to eight weeks from the time all required information has been received.
